name: Victor Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Victor. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We don't have ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the storm-response crew at the Calder Bend depot, down on the river flats where the old mills used to be. On a quiet day we do planned work, replacing old poles, upgrading transformers for all the new heat pumps. On a bad day, when the river wind comes through, we're out for twenty hours restringing lines and resetting breakers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Here's the thing I love: I built a little model, with help from an AI assistant, that looks at the weather forecast and our old fault records and tells me which lines are most likely to come down. Last spring it called five out of seven. What wears me out is that I'm paid less than crews upriver for the same work, and I can't easily switch because there's no other depot within an hour.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mira, my partner. She works at a phone-company call centre on the ring road, answering complaints all day. We rent a flat with a balcony that's mostly full of my tools, and we're saving up, very slowly, after I spent most of what we had on a battery installer course last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold. I'd still be posting my storm model stuff in the lineworkers' forum, because it works. I'd tell the doubters at the depot they were half right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved for Mira, honestly. Her call centre's been talking about chatbots for a year. For me it'd be fine, my job's safe either way, and I'd keep tinkering with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, and keep using AI for my storm planning. I'd start the battery installation side jobs on weekends now that I've got the certificate, maybe two a month at a few hundred each. That would finally put some money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little disappointed I don't get to play with bigger toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the battery course. Why did you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone round here is putting solar panels and home batteries in, and the installers are booked for months. I figured with my electrical background I could do weekend jobs. It cost nearly everything we'd saved, which Mira wasn't thrilled about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mira think of your AI tinkering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's sweet and a bit nerdy. She doesn't love AI, because at work it's the thing that might replace her. So I try not to go on about it at dinner.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, and I'd keep posting my storm model in the lineworkers' forum because it works. I'd tell the doubters at the depot they were half right.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved for Mira, because her call centre has been talking about chatbots for a year. For me it'd be fine, and I'd keep tinkering with the tools.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for storm planning at work and starts weekend battery installation jobs, about two a month at a few hundred each. Uses that money to rebuild the savings he spent on his installer course.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment that the tools don't get bigger.
S0.quote: I'd tell the doubters at the depot they were half right.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is a curious, numbers-minded crew lead who built his own storm prediction model with AI help. His savings are thin because he spent them on a battery installer course, a bet on side income. His partner's call centre job is his real worry, even in the calmest scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where people who learn the tools do well, so learn the tools. I'd be telling the younger guys at the depot to start now. Online I'd be the guy sharing tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. But Mira's call centre is exactly the kind of job that shrinks in this picture. If she loses her job, we're on one lowish wage with nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on the weekend battery jobs, maybe four a month, to build a cushion fast. I'd sit with Mira and look at what she could move into, maybe the training for scheduling at our depot, since she's great on the phone and good under pressure. And I'd ask head office to let me run a proper trial of my storm model across the region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for Mira than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mira if her team got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got this, and I'd mean it, but I'd also say let's not wait. She tends to sit with things, I tend to jump. Between us we usually land somewhere sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Calder Bend is cheap and close to her mum. I'd only move if both of us had something better lined up somewhere else.

S1.say: This is the version where people who learn the tools do well, so learn the tools. I'd tell the younger guys at the depot to start now and I'd share tips online.
S1.think: I'd be fine, maybe better than fine, but Mira's call centre is exactly the kind of job that shrinks here. If she loses it, we're on one lowish wage with nothing in the bank.
S1.do: Pushes his weekend battery jobs up to about four a month to build a cushion fast and helps his partner look at moving into depot scheduling. Asks head office to trial his storm model across the region.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for his partner than for himself.
S1.quote: She tends to sit with things, I tend to jump. Between us we usually land somewhere sensible.
S1.fieldNote: His own job feels safe to him, so his unease is entirely about his partner's exposed call centre job. He responds by doubling his side income rather than cutting back. He's pragmatic and doesn't blame anyone, he just sees where the risk sits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's nobody's fault exactly, but somebody needs to catch the people falling. Government, companies, whoever has the money. I'd still say learn the tools, but I'd admit that's not enough on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one is a real problem for us. Mira's job would go in the first wave, I'd have maybe a year or two before robots start doing the easy line work, and we've got nothing saved. Even my battery side jobs would get hit, because a robot installer would be cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply right away for anything on the grid control or robot supervision side, even if it meant moving to the city. I'd do as many battery jobs as I could in the next twelve months while people still want a human. We'd cut back to basics, cancel the streaming and the second phone line, and Mira would look for work with me wherever we go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the guy who sees the opening, and I'm not sure I see one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the capital, where the control centres are. We'd lose Mira's mum being down the road and pay double the rent. I'd only do it if the job paid enough to make the sums work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years of warning take from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build the cushion. With two years, my side business is just getting started when it gets wiped out. I'd be sprinting with nothing under me.

S2.say: It's nobody's fault exactly, but somebody needs to catch the people falling, whether government or companies. I'd still say learn the tools, but I'd admit that's not enough.
S2.think: This one is a real problem for us, because Mira's job goes in the first wave and robots start on the easy line work within a year or two. We've got nothing saved, and even my battery jobs would get hit.
S2.do: Applies right away for grid control or robot supervision roles, even if it means moving to the city. Does as many battery jobs as possible in the first year and cuts household spending to basics.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because he normally sees the opening and isn't sure he does here.
S2.quote: I'm usually the guy who sees the opening, and I'm not sure I see one.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-comfortable person can be alarmed when the household has no savings and two exposed incomes. He still acts fast, but admits learning the tools isn't enough. Moving to the capital is on the table only if the sums work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd be telling everyone at the depot to pick one new skill this year. I'd probably start a group chat for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but okay. Five years is enough for Mira to retrain, for me to get into the robot side, and for the battery jobs to build up savings. It's tight, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd sign up for the robotics technician course at the regional college and keep doing battery jobs on weekends. I'd help Mira get into a training scheme, maybe medical scheduling or something that still needs a human voice. I'd aim for three months of savings by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Busy, more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a group chat. Who would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger guys at the depot, mostly, and anyone older who's curious. Somebody like Hamid, who's fifty and still asks me how to send photos from his phone, would be welcome. I'd rather drag people along than watch them get left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change things compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm running. Five years, I'm planning. I still think it's coming fast, but now I can get there in time.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd tell everyone at the depot to pick one new skill this year, and I'd start a group chat for it.
S3.think: I'd be anxious but okay, because five years is enough for Mira to retrain, for me to get into the robot side and for my battery jobs to build savings. It's tight, but it's a plan.
S3.do: Signs up for the robotics technician course at the regional college in year one and keeps doing battery jobs on weekends. Helps his partner into a training scheme and aims for three months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, more busy than scared.
S3.quote: I'd rather drag people along than watch them get left.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his alarm into a busy plan for both himself and his partner. He'd take others along, even older colleagues who struggle with phones. His side income remains central to his strategy for building a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if you use it. People should be planning careers, not panicking. I'd be the guy at the depot running the training sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out of this well. I'd be thirty-seven, with years on the robot and control side, and maybe a small battery installation business with a robot or two of my own. Mira would have time to find her next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using AI every day, and over the next few years I'd do the robotics course. I'd grow the battery side jobs and, once the savings are there, buy better tools and maybe a van. I'd help Mira choose a new direction without rushing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, mostly because of Mira, but mostly fine. It feels like something I could actually get good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a robot or two of your own. Are you serious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half serious. If robots get cheap enough, a small installer who knows the wiring and can manage a couple of robots could do well. I'd rather be the guy who owns one than the guy it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with the other two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets us both land on our feet. With two years we'd be scrambling. With five we'd make it, but tired. With ten I can actually build something.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if you use it, so people should be planning careers, not panicking. I'd be the guy at the depot running the training sessions.
S4.think: I think I'd come out of this well, at thirty-seven with years on the robot side and maybe a small battery business with a robot or two. Mira would have time to find her next thing.
S4.do: Keeps his job and uses AI daily while taking the robotics course over the next few years. Grows the battery side business, buys better tools and maybe a van once savings allow, and helps his partner choose a new direction.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with some unease about his partner, and a sense that he could get good at this.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the guy who owns one than the guy it replaces.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he's thinking like a small business owner, not just a worker. His remaining unease is about his partner rather than himself. He sees robots as something he could own and manage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mira and I would both get hit at once with nothing saved. What would help is real money for retraining, not just courses, and some help for couples where both jobs go at once, because that's when people really fall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the partner's job. Everyone asks about mine, and mine is probably safer than hers. My worry has never been the poles, it's the call centre on the ring road.

headlineQuote: My worry has never been the poles, it's the call centre on the ring road.
portrait: Victor Young is a 27-year-old storm-response crew lead at a river-flats depot who uses AI every day and built his own model to predict which lines will fail. He spent most of his savings on a battery installer course, betting on weekend side jobs. His partner Mira works in a call centre, and her exposure drives most of his worry. He stays calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady scenario, and alarmed by AGI in two years, but with five or ten years he plans to retrain, grow his side business and maybe own robots of his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he and his partner would both lose income at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Real money for retraining, not just courses, and help for couples where both jobs disappear at the same time.
